name: Çanakkale
title: Çanakkale Dardanelles Ship Gauging | Anchorage UTM
description: Ultrasonic thickness gauging at Çanakkale and Dardanelles anchorages: bulk carriers, tankers and cargo ships waiting for transit, port calls, pre-docking.
h1: Thickness Measurement for Ships in the Dardanelles at Çanakkale
intro: Çanakkale stands on the narrowest part of the Dardanelles, where every ship moving between the Aegean and the Sea of Marmara passes within sight of the town. Many wait at the strait's anchorages for pilots, daylight or a favourable current, and others call at the local quays for cargo. Those waits and calls give a window for gauging. Technicians travel from India to the ship, boarding at a berth or by launch at anchor.

highlights.p: Ships queue at the Dardanelles anchorages for pilotage and transit slots. A wait of several hours to a day or more can fit a prioritised scope of deck, hatch and tank readings, provided the ship can be released at short notice.
The strait carries strong current and the wind funnels along it. We plan transfers with the agent around the weather and the tide, and order readings so the most important ones come first.
Çanakkale and nearby private quays take bulk cargo for industry, ceramics and the power sector, so ships alongside stay long enough for hold and deck gauging after discharge.

p: The Dardanelles run for about sixty kilometres between the Aegean and the Sea of Marmara, narrowing sharply near Çanakkale, where the channel is only a few kilometres wide. Surface water flows towards the Aegean and a deeper layer moves the other way, and the resulting current, plus winds that follow the line of the strait, make the water around the town lively. The crossing is marked by the Çanakkale 1915 Bridge to the north and by the car ferries that link the town to the opposite shore. Ships entering from the Aegean pass the town on their way to the Marmara, and southbound ships do the reverse.

Transit is managed by the Turkish Straits vessel traffic service and carried out under pilotage in the manner set by the Montreux Convention, and the order in which ships pass depends on traffic, size and the time of day. Large or deep-draught ships, loaded tankers among them, may be held at anchor until their turn. The anchorages near the strait therefore hold a changing population of bulk carriers, tankers, container ships and general cargo ships, some staying only for a pilot and others for much longer, and that churn is the practical basis for most gauging requests.

Çanakkale itself is a regional port rather than a major cargo gateway. Its quays and the private terminals along the strait handle bulk materials for local industry, including raw material for ceramics and building products, as well as fuel and general cargo, and the coast also supports fishing and small-craft traffic. Small yards and slipways around the strait serve tugs, workboats and coasters, though a full drydock for larger merchant ships is not available here, so heavier work normally goes to the Marmara yards or to ports in the Aegean.

facilities.h: Where a ship can be gauged at Çanakkale
p: The anchorages are the most useful venue, as well as the most demanding. A ship at anchor can be boarded by launch arranged through the agent, then worked while it waits. The tidal stream through the strait makes the ship swing and the launch's approach difficult at some states of the current, so the agent's local advice decides the timing of each transfer. A prioritised scope keeps the job useful even if the ship is called to move: deck plating, hatch covers and coamings, air pipes, ballast tanks that the crew has prepared and certified, and any item raised by a recent inspection.

Alongside, the scope widens. At the commercial quay and the private terminals, bulk carriers can have holds gauged once cargo is out and the crew has cleaned them. Tanker work is limited to deck, certified ballast tanks and deck piping unless cargo tanks are cleaned and gas-free. For ships that need a dry hull, the plan is to gauge at Çanakkale first and send the readings ahead to a yard on the Marmara or in the Aegean, so the steel estimate is ready when the ship is booked in. A short job at Çanakkale can therefore be one stage of a longer programme.
list: Dardanelles anchorages — deck, hatch cover, air pipe and ballast tank gauging on ships waiting for pilots or transit slots, reached by launch
Çanakkale town quays — bulk and general cargo ships gauged after discharge, with holds, coamings and decks on the list
Private terminals along the strait — hold and deck gauging on bulk carriers serving industrial plants, within each terminal's rules
Fuel and liquid berths — deck, deck piping and certified ballast tanks on small tankers
Small yard slipways and repair quays — tugs, workboats and coasters gauged when hauled out or alongside for repair
Handover to a Marmara or Aegean yard — readings carried forward into a docking steel estimate

context.h: The Turkish Straits regime and port state control
p: Ships transiting the Dardanelles and calling at Çanakkale come under Turkey's maritime authorities, with the Ministry of Transport and Infrastructure and the harbour master responsible for port state control under the Black Sea and Mediterranean MoUs. The Directorate General of Coastal Safety runs the traffic service and pilotage for the strait. Ships that arrive here have often just come from the Black Sea or from an Aegean port where an inspector has already looked at them, so deficiency records from the previous call are worth reading before planning a scope at Çanakkale.

For older tonnage on Black Sea and Aegean trades, the strait is a pinch point where waiting time and structural condition meet. A bulk carrier at its fourth renewal survey may sit at the anchorage for hours with wasted hatch coamings that an inspector has already noted, and a superintendent will want readings before the ship reaches the yard. Ships bound for EU ports must carry a valid Inventory of Hazardous Materials and are subject to carbon reporting there, so owners keep gauging records current for the hull file.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs at Çanakkale
jobs.p: Çanakkale jobs split between short anchorage scopes and fuller programmes alongside. The anchorage work is driven by a transit delay that the owner decides to use, and is planned with a clear understanding that the ship may be told to proceed. Berth work follows cargo discharge or fits into a regional port call. Several jobs are preparation for a docking that is booked at a Marmara or Aegean yard.
list: Deck, hatch cover and coaming gauging on a bulk carrier waiting at anchor for a northbound transit after port state control recorded wasted coamings.
Ballast tank and air pipe gauging on a product tanker held at the Dardanelles anchorage before a Marmara discharge.
Hold frame and hopper plate gauging on a Supramax bulk carrier alongside at a private terminal after discharging industrial raw material.
Pre-docking gauging on an older general cargo ship at the town quay, so a Marmara yard can order steel before the ship arrives.
Condition gauging on a coaster after hauling out at a small yard on the strait, with shell plating and sea chests on the list.
Pre-purchase gauging on a second-hand bulk carrier at anchor, with the buyer's surveyor present.

logistics: Çanakkale has a domestic airport, but most travel runs through Istanbul, with the team continuing by road around the Marmara or along the Gelibolu peninsula, or by sea and ferry connections where convenient. The ship's agent arranges quay passes, launches for the anchorages and the terminal's gas-free and permit requirements, and receives crew lists, technician certificates and equipment details beforehand. Technicians from India need a Turkish visa, and because strait delays are unpredictable, we apply early and keep the visa period flexible.

faqs.q: Can you gauge a ship waiting at the Dardanelles anchorage?
faqs.a: Yes, by launch booked through the agent. Strait traffic can release the ship with little notice, so we agree a priority list with the master and superintendent and take the most important readings first. Deck, hatch covers, coamings, air pipes and ballast tanks the crew has certified are the usual targets, depending on the current and the sea.

faqs.q: How does the current affect launch transfers?
faqs.a: The Dardanelles carry a strong stream, and ships at anchor swing with it. The agent's pilots and launch operators know which states of the current make boarding awkward, and we follow their advice on timing. If conditions are poor the transfer is postponed rather than forced, and the scope is trimmed to what remains.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock at Çanakkale?
faqs.a: Not for larger merchant ships. Small yards and slipways around the strait handle tugs, workboats and coasters, but ships that need a dry hull normally go to a Marmara yard or to an Aegean port. Readings taken here are reported in a form that can go straight to the yard to support the steel estimate.

faqs.q: Can holds be gauged on a bulk carrier at a local quay?
faqs.a: Yes, after the cargo is discharged and the holds are cleaned enough for entry. We measure frames, hopper and tank top plating and hatch coamings, and we agree the sequence with the chief officer so the holds are returned in time for the next cargo.
